query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of a ductility‐promoting element (e.g., ~5–10 at% Ti) to equal‐atomic BCC NbMoTaW will induce a controlled dual‐phase microstructure (a continuous BCC matrix with discrete, ductile secondary precipitates) that improves room‐temperature ductility and enhances irradiation defect recombination while preserving the high‐temperature strength and overall BCC stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW known for excellent high-temperature mechanical properties but poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of Ti (or a similar ductility‐enhancing element) during alloy synthesis to trigger limited phase separation into a dual-phase microstructure.
generation.conditions: Tested at room temperature (for ductility improvement) and at elevated temperatures up to 1600 °C; irradiation experiments performed under helium implantation conditions simulating reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase structure where a ductile secondary phase (e.g., B2 or a Ti-enriched region) is finely dispersed within the continuous BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Ti addition is expected to lower dislocation core energy and enhance slip system activation, thereby increasing room-temperature plasticity. Simultaneously, the presence of dispersed secondary phase boundaries can act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects and facilitate self-healing via enhanced atomic diffusion and defect recombination, all while retaining the overall BCC structural stability required for high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-doped alloy should exhibit a marked improvement in room-temperature ductility (i.e. higher total plastic strain before failure) with minimal compromise of its high-temperature yield strength (maintained near 1600 °C) and will display reduced irradiation-induced defect accumulation, blistering, or amorphization under helium implantation.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with excellent high-temperature strength but very limited ductility at room temperature, and irradiated behavior inferred primarily from computational studies.
generation.boundary: The ductility enhancement is expected primarily at room temperature (up to ~800 °C) while the high-temperature mechanical benefits are maintained up to ~1600 °C; similarly, the improved irradiation resistance is targeted under helium irradiation conditions relevant to nuclear applications.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti concentration and processing conditions to achieve the desired dual-phase microstructure without compromising high-temperature behavior remain to be precisely determined. Long-term phase stability under extended irradiation and thermal cycling also requires further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set of equal-atomic NbMoTaW (control) and a second set of NbMoTaW with 5–10 at% Ti addition. Use identical processing routes to achieve homogeneous starting microstructures. Characterize the phase composition and microstructure by XRD and high-resolution TEM to verify the presence of a continuous BCC matrix with discrete Ti-enriched (ductile) precipitates. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) creep or compression tests to compare mechanical properties. Also, conduct helium irradiation (simulated reactor fluences) followed by nanoindentation and defect analysis (via TEM/APT) to compare irradiation-induced damage.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile ductility (% strain to failure)
Yield strength at elevated temperatures (e.g., at 1600 °C)
Microstructural phase analysis (XRD, TEM) verifying dual-phase formation
Irradiation-induced hardening or defect density via nanoindentation/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped NbMoTaW alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., a notable increase in plastic strain compared to the control) without compromising its high-temperature yield strength, or if irradiation studies do not reveal enhanced defect recombination (i.e., similar or worse irradiation-induced hardening/defect accumulation compared to baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Intrinsic factors responsible for brittle versus ductile nature of refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. Our findings demonstrate how ductility and strength can be controlled through the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in RHEAs.Subject terms: M

Microstructural Design for Improving Ductility of An Initially Brittle Refractory High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.
